purpose: Icatibant is used to treat sudden attacks of a condition called hereditary angioedema (HAE), which causes severe swelling under the skin, in the belly, or in the throat. It helps relieve these painful and potentially dangerous swelling episodes in adults and children. It does not prevent attacks from happening, but it treats them when they do occur.
how_it_works: When an HAE attack happens, your body releases too much of a chemical called bradykinin, which causes fluid to leak out of blood vessels and leads to swelling. Icatibant works by blocking the spot in your body where bradykinin attaches, kind of like putting a plug in a lock so the key cannot get in. By blocking bradykinin, the medication stops the swelling from getting worse and helps it go away.
common_side_effects: The most common side effects happen right where the injection is given and include redness, swelling, itching, burning, or bruising at the injection site. These reactions are usually mild and go away on their own. Some people may also feel dizzy, have a fever, or notice a rash.
warnings: If you are having an attack that involves throat swelling, go to the emergency room right away even after using this medication, because throat swelling can be life-threatening. Tell your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, as the safety in these situations is not fully established. Do not use icatibant if you are allergic to any of its ingredients.
typical_dosing: The usual dose is one injection of 30 mg given under the skin (subcutaneous injection) during an HAE attack. If symptoms do not improve after 6 hours, a second dose may be given, and a third dose can be given 6 hours after that if needed, up to a maximum of 3 doses in 24 hours. Your doctor or nurse will show you how to give the injection yourself so you can treat attacks quickly at home.
